author: Yash Watwani
text:
ML Engineer vs AI Engineer: they are not the same thing

A lot of people use these titles like they’re interchangeable.

They’re not.

Here’s the simple version:

ML Engineer
- builds and deploys machine learning systems
- works with training pipelines, features, inference, evaluation, monitoring
- usually cares a lot about model performance, reliability, and productionization

AI Engineer
- builds applications around LLMs and foundation models
- works with prompts, RAG, agents, tool use, orchestration, guardrails, evaluation
- usually cares a lot about product behavior, response quality, latency, and trust

The overlap is real.  
But the focus is different.

If you are interviewing or hiring, this distinction matters because:
- one role is often more model/system heavy
- the other is often more application/workflow heavy

The biggest mistake I see is people preparing for one role and applying to the other.

author: Bradley Mileham
text:
🚀 People keep putting Quantum, AI, and Web3 into the same "next big thing" bucket.

I don't think they belong there.

🤖 AI

AI hiring is booming... but only for specialists.

ML Systems, AI Infrastructure, and GPU Engineers are in huge demand, while many general software engineering roles have become far more competitive.

The demand isn't for AI in general, it's for people with deep, specialised expertise.

⛓️ Web3

Web3 is the one people still get wrong. Over 70 crypto projects have disappeared in H1 2026 alone, funding has consolidated, and capital is flowing to a much smaller number of winners.

Yet the demand for Protocol Engineers, Distributed Systems Engineers, Cryptographers, ZK, and Security specialists remains. The market hasn't disappeared; it's become far more selective.

⚛️ Quantum

Quantum has the opposite problem: the demand is there, but the talent simply isn't.

There are only a small number of experienced researchers and engineers working in areas like QEC, quantum hardware, control systems and quantum software, meaning many companies are competing for the same people.

The bottleneck isn't funding, it's expertise.

💡 Different markets. Same lesson.

The engineers who continue to get hired aren't chasing trends. They're building deep expertise in difficult technical problems.

Whether that's Quantum, AI, or Web3, specialist knowledge continues to win.

Chase the skill, not the label.

author: Pranay Mahendrakar
text:
Not every AI user is a Fortune 500 company. Some of the most rewarding work I've done is for small businesses.

A local restaurant wanted to predict daily ingredient needs to reduce food waste. We built a simple time-series model using their POS data and local event calendars. Food waste dropped 35%.

A small e-commerce shop wanted product descriptions in multiple languages. A fine-tuned translation model generates descriptions in 5 languages from a single English input. Their international sales doubled.

A photography studio wanted to automatically sort and tag 50,000 photos. A vision model + simple clustering does it in hours instead of weeks of manual work.

None of these required cutting-edge AI. A gradient boosted tree. A fine-tuned translation model. A pre-trained vision backbone.

The tech was simple. The impact was enormous for businesses operating on thin margins.

What small businesses need from AI isn't a sophisticated architecture. It's a reliable solution that saves them time or money, doesn't require a PhD to maintain, and costs less than hiring another person.

If you can build these kinds of solutions, the market is massive and largely untapped. There are millions of small businesses that could benefit from basic ML but don't know where to start.

Be the engineer who makes AI accessible, not just impressive.

Adding “GenAI, LLMs, Agentic AI” without being able to explain what you built.

Very few candidates can answer the follow-up questions.

 • Why RAG instead of fine-tuning?
 • How did you evaluate your model’s performance?
 • What did you do to reduce hallucinations?
 • How did you optimize latency and inference costs?
 • How did you measure the business impact of your solution?

That’s what separates someone who has learned AI from someone who can engineer AI.

If you’re targeting high-paying Data Scientist, ML Engineer, or Applied AI Engineer roles in 2026, your preparation needs to reflect what companies are actually hiring for.

Instead of cloning another chatbot:

→ Build AI systems that solve real business problems.
→ Learn RAG, vector databases, and retrieval pipelines.
→ Work with agent orchestration and multi-agent workflows.
→ Design evaluation pipelines to measure model quality.
→ Deploy production-ready AI applications.
→ Understand scalability, latency, security, and cost optimization.
→ Most importantly, learn to connect every technical decision to a measurable business outcome.

These are the discussions that make interviewers believe you can build AI in the real world—not just follow tutorials.

The demand for AI talent is growing rapidly, but companies are becoming far more selective.

They’re looking for engineers who can design, build, evaluate, and deploy reliable AI systems that create business value.

That’s why more professionals are moving away from scattered learning and choosing structured, industry-focused preparation.

At Tutort Academy, they’ve helped 2,800+ professionals transition into high-paying product-based companies through real-world GenAI projects, production-focused learning, mock interviews, and mentorship from engineers working at leading tech companies.

The AI opportunities in 2026 won’t go to the people with the most buzzwords on their resumes.

They’ll go to the people who can confidently explain what they built, why they built it, and the impact it created.
